teacher_issue: Atomizer aspiration versus pressurization
teacher_scientific_note: Source D is supported by printed NBF p.101: squeezing the air bulb drives faster airflow across the vertical pickup opening; lower local static pressure relative to liquid surface allows higher exterior pressure to raise perfume. This is aspirating action, not a decrease in gravity or increase in perfume density.

teacher_issue: Filter pump loses suction with weak water flow
teacher_scientific_note: The original NBF p.101–102 water-jet filter pump uses the jet to form a low-pressure region by the side tube. Weaker flow generally weakens entrainment/pressure reduction, so source C is best; a detailed real pump also depends on nozzle geometry, losses and surrounding pressure.

teacher_issue: Local pressure–air speed claim requires controlled comparison
teacher_scientific_note: Source A is a defensible general tendency for similar atomizer geometry and operating conditions: stronger fast airflow may reduce local static pressure near the nozzle. It is not a universal pressure-speed identity for arbitrary flows. Distinguish formative B39 basic effect from B44 application analysis.

teacher_issue: Greater depth increases ideal efflux speed
teacher_scientific_note: For an open large tank with pressure cancellation, negligible surface speed and negligible losses, v=sqrt(2gh) increases with the vertical free-surface-to-orifice head h, so source D is correct. Compare openings at the same liquid surface level.

teacher_issue: Free-surface speed is a continuity approximation
teacher_scientific_note: In a tank with A_tank much larger than A_hole, the quasi-steady incompressible volume balance gives v_surface=(A_hole/A_tank)*v_exit, so source D. As the tank drains the surface is not literally stationary, and this primarily tests continuity B36 rather than individually satisfying B40 Bernoulli Application.

teacher_issue: Equal atmospheric boundary pressures
teacher_scientific_note: An open tank free surface and a free jet discharging into the same atmosphere both have P_atm, so these pressure terms cancel in the ideal Bernoulli equation, source B. Neither atmosphere nor absolute pressure is zero; source teacher A-level tag needs independent cognitive signoff.

teacher_issue: Density cancels only in ideal same-fluid derivation
teacher_scientific_note: Under the textbook ideal single-liquid open tank with equal boundary atmospheric pressures, rho*g*h converts to rho*v²/2, so rho cancels and v=sqrt(2gh), source B. Density dependence can reappear when losses or different exterior pressure conditions matter.

teacher_issue: Comparison with free-fall speed is printed
teacher_scientific_note: Original printed NBF p.102–103 compares Torricelli efflux to free fall through the same height using v²=2gh. Source B is correct; recognizing this analogy alone is an Understanding prerequisite, not necessarily a full B40 Application problem.

teacher_issue: Zero head is a limiting ideal result
teacher_scientific_note: With the opening level equal to the free surface, h=0 and the ideal square-root relation gives v=0 (D). This is the no-driving-head mathematical limit for an open unpressurized tank, not a claim that all outlet flows at zero geometric head are impossible with external pressure or pumps.

teacher_issue: Real Torricelli discharge needs head-loss correction
teacher_scientific_note: Viscosity, contraction and other dissipative effects can lower actual outlet speed below sqrt(2gh) for given hydrostatic head. Source D is correct. NBF p.102 ideal assumptions differ from real flow; B41 viscosity is a distinct Summative/Understanding outcome and this conceptual limitation is not automatically B40 Application.

teacher_issue: Wider section lower speed and higher static pressure
teacher_scientific_note: For steady incompressible lossless horizontal flow through a fixed Venturi meter, the wider section has lower mean speed and greater static pressure by continuity and Bernoulli. Original D correct; real meter pressure differences include head losses and do not imply the same pressures in every flow regime.

teacher_issue: Pressure difference alone is not sufficient to determine flow rate
teacher_scientific_note: Source B is the best method among offered options: measured wide/throat pressure difference permits inference using ideal Bernoulli plus continuity. Quantitative speed or volume-flow calculation also requires geometry (area ratio), fluid density and assumptions about losses; note these before classifying as B44 Application.

teacher_issue: Fixed Q inverse area is continuity rather than Bernoulli
teacher_scientific_note: Source C follows v_throat=Q/A_throat when inlet volume rate Q is fixed. This is an explicit area-speed continuity computation, candidate B36; it does not independently explain the Venturi pressure drop required for a B44 device analysis or full B40 Bernoulli Application.

teacher_issue: Equal heights cancel gravitational terms but do not remove gravity
teacher_scientific_note: For a horizontal Venturi, h1=h2 and rho*g*h1=rho*g*h2, so source C. The teacher source labels this Application, but choosing the cancellation reason is predominantly conceptual Understanding until individual FBISE cognitive mapping is approved.

teacher_issue: Venturi carburetor fuel aspiration under pressure difference
teacher_scientific_note: Original printed NBF p.104 illustrated carburetor places fuel supply near a narrow fast air passage; pressure reduction encourages petrol flow, so source D. Real automotive fuel delivery can involve jets, metering and other components; do not infer petrol attraction by a magnetic force.

teacher_issue: Original Figure6.14 is simplified; reject equal-transit-time myth
teacher_scientific_note: The printed p.104 Figure6.14 labels lower pressure above and higher pressure below the depicted aerofoil, making source B correct for that illustration. The diagram also shows longer/shorter paths, which must NOT be taught as an equal-arrival-time requirement. Public source record contains no referenceFigureId; confirm student-facing illustration fidelity separately before figure-dependent certification.

teacher_issue: Lift direction from pressure gradient is simpler than full device analysis
teacher_scientific_note: For a simplified wing with larger mean static pressure below than above, the net pressure contribution is upward, original B. Actual wing force is the integrated pressure and shear over all surfaces; the teacher labels this Understanding, not automatically B44 Summative/Application analysis.

teacher_issue: Magnus transverse force explanation needs flow context
teacher_scientific_note: Spin can alter the flow and pressure distribution, producing a transverse aerodynamic force, source D. Original NBF p.105 depicts Magnus flow around rotating body. The item is Understanding; official B44 Application requires individual evidence of analysing how spin changes a real trajectory.

teacher_issue: Reversing spin may reverse deflection direction
teacher_scientific_note: With same ball motion and otherwise similar aerodynamics, reversing spin changes the sense of flow asymmetry and may reverse transverse Magnus force, source B. The word may is scientifically important because detailed force depends on spin axis, relative wind and surface conditions.

teacher_issue: Two-sheet experiment alone is Bernoulli-effect demonstration
teacher_scientific_note: The textbook's p.101 sheet experiment finds faster air between sheets associated with lower interior static pressure; exterior pressure pushes inward, source A. As a standalone ideal effect explanation it closely reflects formative B39, not automatically the Application-level real-world device analysis of summative B44; keep as practice unless independently mapped.
